papers.title: Contact-number hyperuniformity at glass close packing in infinite dimensions
papers.abstract: We investigate contact-number fluctuations of harmonic spheres near glass close packing (GCP), the amorphous jamming endpoint reached by compressing an ideal glass. Using replica theory, we show that the Gardner-unstable region shrinks toward jamming as the spatial dimension increases, allowing GCP to be approached along a stable one-step replica symmetry breaking branch in the high-dimensional limit. By coupling an external field to the local contact number, we derive the variance of the total contact number and the wave-number-dependent structure factor directly from the microscopic interactions. At GCP, the structure factor vanishes quadratically at small scaled wave numbers, demonstrating contact-number hyperuniformity. Upon weak compression above GCP, the structure factor develops a low-wave-number plateau whose height is proportional to the excess coordination. These results provide an analytical description of contact-number hyperuniformity and its breakdown upon compression.

papers.title: On the richness of metamaterials generated by recursive cell division
papers.abstract: Scale-rich metamaterials are one member of a family of recursive cell divisions, which differ in which cell is cut, where the cut passes and at what angle. We characterise six members of this family through three network mappings, the cell tree, the dual graph of ligaments and junctions, and the frame graph of spans, and through their elastic-wave properties: the effective refractive index n, its isotropy and the band over which it holds. The dual-graph degree law, the mean degree and the age law of the ligaments hit by new ones are the same for every rule, so they cannot distinguish the materials. The cell tree and the cell shapes do differ, and one consequence of them explains the physics: the tail of long spans in the frame graph. With the longest spans as the length scale, the bending part of the inverse squared index follows a single power law across rules, densities and numbers of ligaments, and the same spans set the lowest local resonance and the band edge. The stretching part, which caps the index, is carried by the straight frame lines of the tiling rather than by the division. Random cut angles produce elongated cells and long spans, hence high index and a narrow band; cuts perpendicular to the long axis of the cell keep the cells compact, giving low index and a wide band. Cutting through the centroid instead of a random point bounds the split fraction between 4/9 and 5/9, which removes the area hierarchy without changing the index. The cut angle interpolates continuously between these limits, and the isotropy peaks where the ligament orientations become isotropic while the cells are still compact. In three dimensions the plate and strut divisions are stretching dominated and the index stays low for every rule.

papers.title: Why do continual physical learners need sleep?
papers.abstract: Sleep is widespread across the animal kingdom, including in organisms without a centralized nervous system. Does learning create a need for sleep, even without biology? To explore this question, we study a disordered spring network trained to perform a sequence of mechanical allosteric tasks through local changes in bond stiffness. We find that continual learning progressively reduces the network's ability to acquire new tasks as individual bonds become increasingly specialized. We identify an exact algebraic relationship between the polarization of bond dominance and the network's remaining learning capacity, providing a quantitative measure of this loss of adaptability. We then demonstrate that random internal perturbations allow individual bonds to estimate their mechanical dominance and locally adjust their stiffnesses to restore learning capacity. However, the forces associated with active learning bias these local measurements and interfere with restoration. Separating learning and repair into wake-like and sleep-like phases removes this interference and improves continual-learning performance. Our results suggest that the need for offline restorative phases can emerge from the mechanics of physical learning, even in systems without biological components.

papers.title: Apparent contact angle equation for a dielectric droplet on a conductive hydrophilic surface in an electric field
papers.abstract: A dielectric droplet resting on a conductive substrate elongates when a voltage is applied across the surrounding gap without touching the upper electrode. We construct a closed form theory of the equilibrium shapes by approximating the interface as a truncated spheroid with a single shape parameter and obtain the dimensionless electrostatic prefactor that corrects the free-space depolarization, based on the mirror symmetry across the substrate. Minimizing the resulting free energy along voltage ramps reproduces the boundary-element-method (BEM) equilibria, both the droplet height and the contact-line radius, with and without gravity, at negligible computational cost. An explicit apparent contact angle equation is found that collapses all the numerical calculation data. The configuration shows a behavior of fixed contact angle and an increasing apparent angle with the applied voltage, which is completely different from that of the Young--Lippmann equation.

papers.title: Universal scaling of brine migration in ice
papers.abstract: Sea ice hosts mobile brine inclusions whose migration influences salt redistribution, microstructure and transport within the ice. Although their motion under temperature gradient is commonly described as a diffusion-limited process, experimental evidence has remained rare and insufficient because migration is slow and controlled inclusion seeding is challenging. Here we introduce an experimental method to trap and monitor hundreds of inclusions in ice under controlled temperature gradients. Using four solutes, three imposed gradients and two order of magnitude in initial concentration, we quantify migration dynamics over a broad range of conditions. We find that, except close to the ice front, inclusion migration is consistent with a regime limited by solute diffusion. After applying a universal scaling, both our data and previous measurements collapse onto a master curve, providing a general framework for describing solute transport in ice.

papers.title: Indentation of pre-tensioned cortex-like fibre networks: tension, local stretching and the signature of defect architecture
papers.abstract: Indentation is widely used to infer the mechanical state of biological materials like the actomyosin cortex. It reduces a single force-indentation curve to an apparent modulus. The cortex, however, is a pre-tensioned, heterogeneous fibre network. We show that this inference is ambiguous. The same amount of weakening can leave the indentation force unchanged or lower it tenfold, depending on where it lies relative to the probe. The force reflects how the probe couples to the tensioned, load-bearing structure, not the amount of weakening. We combine molecular dynamics simulations of a pressure-loaded, crosslinked fibre network indented by a rigid sphere with a continuum membrane solution. We represent the simulated force-depth response by a two-term fit, $F\propto a\delta+b\delta^{3/2}$, with $a$ reflecting the global tension, and $b$ the stiffening with depth. At a fixed fraction of weakened bonds, diffuse weakening lowers the force by a factor of about 1.5. A weak cluster beneath the probe lowers it 8-12-fold, because the slack cluster decouples the probe from the tension. When the clusters are displaced from the contact, the force returns to within 15% of the healthy value. Two opposite effects cancel. The clusters soften the whole layer, which lowers its tension and the force. But they also channel the load through the intact network beneath the probe, which stiffens it locally and raises the force. The shape of the curve retains what the force level hides. The coefficient $a$ reflects the softened layer when clusters beside the probe keep the force near the healthy value. The local exponent $\alpha=\mathrm{d}\ln F/\mathrm{d}\ln\delta$ increases with depth in every configuration except when a cluster lies beneath the probe, where the two-term form no longer applies. Detecting localised weakening requires spatial sampling and analysis of the curve shape, not a single fitted modulus.

papers.title: Magnetic tuning of odd elastic instabilities in chiral active crystals
papers.abstract: We investigate the dynamical properties of an odd active crystal whose elementary units follow an inertial dynamics and experience a Lorentz force induced by an external magnetic field. The continuous injection of energy associated with active chirality gives rise to odd elasticity, manifested through transverse forces between the crystal constituents. We show that the interplay between the magnetic field and these transverse forces produces a distinctive long-wavelength instability at vanishing wavevector, which is absent in both non-magnetic elastic crystals and passive crystals subjected to a magnetic field. Moreover, the magnetic field provides a means of tuning the collective oscillations of the crystal, enabling the emergence of exceptional points and tuning the dynamical instability induced by odd elasticity at finite wavevectors. Our analytical results yield explicit predictions for the displacement spectrum, static structure factor, and intermediate scattering function. These findings suggest that magnetic fields could provide a powerful tool for controlling collective phenomena in high-density systems of granular or colloidal spinners.

papers.title: Accounts on Synthetic Cells
authors: The Frontiers of Life Research Network
papers.abstract: Frontiers of Life is a research network of the University of Bordeaux focused on the re-engineering of living systems, starting from the construction of a synthetic cell. In this article, we present our motivation to build a cell from scratch and the elementary building blocks we worked on over the past four years. While the final objective regarding the construction of a synthetic cell remains a long-term target, the reconstruction of living cells provides both a methodology and experimental approaches to improve our understanding of living systems with potential to become the next generation of biotechnologies.

papers.title: Lie-Poisson Formulation of Dissipative Spin Hydrodynamics
papers.abstract: Covariance and the second law cannot fix how fluid flow couples to spin, since reversible couplings produce no entropy. We show that the spin commutation relations and the Poincar\'e algebra fix these couplings. Reversibly, a flow exerts no torque on the spin: its magnitude per particle is conserved, its direction is Fermi--Walker transported, and spin--shear couplings reflect a deforming triad. The magnitude changes only through higher multipoles, as in spinor condensates, or dissipation, whose first-order spin--shear coupling reorients the spin away from the vorticity above a critical shear rate.

papers.title: A Variational Description of the Adsorption Phenomenon
papers.abstract: The adsorption of particles dispersed in a liquid is analyzed introducing a variational approach. While traditional adsorption models rely on localized, discrete site-binding kinetics, we treat the system as a binary mixture consisting of adsorbate particles (APs) and the host liquid within a continuous framework. An expression for the variation of the mixing entropy arising from an inhomogeneous distribution of the APs, of density $n(z)$ is derived. The interactions between APs are modeled by a bulk free energy functional containing a term proportional to the square of the density, $\nabla n$, and a bulk compressibility term which exhibits a minimum at the equilibrium bulk density of APs, $n_0$, in the absence of adsorption. This approach offers the distinct advantage of capturing non-local fluid structures and particle-particle correlations near interfaces that discrete models overlook. The profile $n(z)$ is obtained analytically by linearization of the Euler-Lagrange equilibrium equation for a sample confined between two parallel walls under the constraint of particles number conservation. The surface density of adsorbed particles, $\sigma$ is then calculated for the simplified case in which the interaction with the substrate is short-ranged and decays exponentially into the bulk. For a semi-infinite sample limited by a planar wall, the analysis predicts that $\sigma\sim n_0$ for small values of $n_0$, whereas it saturates at a constant value for large $n_0$, in agreement with the predictions of the classical Langmuir model, thereby providing a thermodynamic foundation for phenomenological adsorption isotherms. In case a localized surface energy is present, an effective adsorption energy is derived in the limiting cases of vanishing and very large anchoring strength, offering a predictive tool for tailoring surface modifications in experimental soft matter systems.

papers.title: Polymer adsorption on vicinal surfaces
papers.abstract: While polymer adsorption is theoretically well established on flat surfaces --- and somewhat understood on rough surfaces --- the common and practically relevant case of nearly flat stepped surfaces remains poorly studied. Here, we address this gap via extensive simulations of flexible polymer chains grafted at the step edge of vicinal surfaces. For wide terraces, the polymer-step interaction yields a stable step-attached (SA) phase, alongside the desorbed and terrace-adsorbed (TA) phases, all of them separated by continuous transition lines that meet at a multicritical point previously unanticipated in polymer thermodynamics. This scenario is observed for terrace widths $\mathcal{W} \gtrsim 3 R_g^{(2D)}$, being $R_g^{(2D)}$ the radius of gyration of TA polymers. Simpler phase diagrams, absent this multicriticality, are found for $\mathcal{W} \lesssim 3 R_g^{(2D)}$, where a simple crossover exists between the SA and TA phases. The presence of kinks at the steps does not alter these behaviors. Besides their theoretical relevance, these findings unveil an interesting route to produce polymer nanowires and control polymer conformation via step attachment-detachment on designed stepped surfaces.

papers.title: Quasiconformal geometry and elastic anisotropy in liquid crystals
papers.abstract: Unequal splay and bend elastic constants endow planar nematic liquid crystals with a director-dependent anisotropic geometry. Here, we show that this geometry is quasiconformal: the magnitude of the associated Beltrami coefficient is fixed by the elastic constants, while its phase depends on the director relative to a compatible rotating frame introducing an SO(2) spin connection. We construct explicit maps for a hybrid-aligned film and isolated defect textures, generalizing the conformal construction of isotropic defects. These results provide a new insight into the classical Dzyaloshinskii defect solutions, which are shown to define an auxiliary reference cone on which the defect texture is quasiconformally distorted before being projected conformally into physical space. Numerical simulations of constrained +2 defects reveal core morphologies consistent with the quasiconformal geometry. Our results suggest that quasiconformal maps provide a broader geometric language for anisotropy in liquid crystals and other materials.

papers.title: Spontaneous axis formation through defect fusion in active nematics
papers.abstract: Initially spherical embryos break symmetry to establish a body axis. Topological defects in tissue nematic order have been implicated in axis formation, but the physical mechanisms underlying defect organization in active materials remain unclear. We study an active nematic fluid on a sphere using a fully covariant hydrodynamic theory that ensures thermodynamic consistency in the passive limit. We find that, in compressible systems, active nematic traction drives a spontaneous transition from the equilibrium configuration of four separated +1/2 defects to two antipodal +1 defects through pairwise fusion. The resulting state defines an axis, with aster or vortex textures at the poles depending on the flow-nematic coupling. These results identify a physical mechanism by which active forces reorganize topological defects to establish an axis on a spherical surface.

papers.title: Interplay of Activity and Attraction in the Coil-to-Globule Transition of Tangentially Driven Polymers
papers.abstract: The coil-to-globule transition is a paradigmatic phenomenon in polymer physics and biophysics, driven by intrachain attractions. However, in biopolymers, attractive interactions coexist with nonequilibrium active processes, leaving open the question of how activity modifies the transition. Using Brownian dynamics simulations of tangentially driven polymers, we show that activity broadens the coil-to-globule crossover without shifting the $\Theta$ point by generating transient pearl-necklace conformations, which delay globule formation. Activity-induced chain backfolding defines an emergent active blob of $g_a$ monomers that together with a thermal blob of $g_T$ monomers govern the transition. From scaling arguments, we identify a new scaling variable based on the ratio $g_a/g_T$ that collapses the gyration-radius expansion factors near the $\Theta$ point onto the master curve of passive polymers across a broad activity range. Our results establish a blob-scaling framework for active polymer collapse.

papers.title: In-plane diffusion, spurious drift and a physics-structured gap predictor for a free colloidal pair
papers.abstract: When the diffusivity of a Brownian particle depends on position, its mean displacement acquires a noise-induced (spurious) drift whose magnitude is set by the stochastic convention $\alpha$. Inspired by the particle-wall experiments published by G. Volpe and co-workers, we ask how much of this physics can be extracted from a pair of 1.95 $\mu$m polystyrene spheres released from blinking holographic optical tweezers at five temperatures between 2 and 40 $^\circ$C. The single-sphere diffusivity inside the pair stays between 0.093 and 0.098 $\mu$m$^2$ s$^{-1}$, whereas the Stokes-Einstein value for water rises from 0.126 to 0.361 $\mu$m$^2$ s$^{-1}$; an isolated sphere shows the same deficit, so the missing diffusivity scale originates in the measurement and not in the pair interaction. The pair is what makes the diffusivity depend on position: from the measured gap-dependent diffusivities $D_\parallel(h)$ and $D_\perp(h)$ we build a Fokker-Planck predictor of the future gap and score it on held-out releases. It recovers the 90% width of the gap distribution up to 800 ms but cannot discriminate between $\alpha = 0$, $1/2$ and $1$, because the $\alpha$-dependent mean shift is an order of magnitude smaller than that width. The ensemble spurious drift is consistent with zero at both ends of the temperature range, and the regression for $\alpha$ never exceeds $R^2 = 0.22$. We present a planar methods baseline and identify the measurements required to resolve $\alpha$.

papers.title: Frustrated Interlayer Coupling Creates a Higher-Order Helical Superstructure in a Twist-Bend Smectic Phase
papers.abstract: Bent liquid-crystalline dimers provide a model system for studying the spontaneous emergence of chirality from achiral molecules. Depending on terminal-chain length, these materials exhibit a competition between heliconical, synclinic, and anticlinic packing tendencies in tilted smectic phases. In short homologues, the tendency to form twist-bend phases dominates, leading to two distinct helical phases: the SmCTB-SH phase, with a helical periodicity of four molecular lengths, and at lower temperatures, a double helical structure - the SmCTB-DH phase, with progressive rotation of the four-layer unit. With increasing terminal chain length, this twist-bend tendency is gradually suppressed, favoring phases with simple synclinic and anticlinic tilt arrangement in successive layers. Remarkably, in the regime where these tendencies become comparable, a new modulated smectic phase, SmCTB-mod develops; a double helical structure in which the internal four-layer unit undergoes a periodic modulation. This additional level of structural organization provides a means of accommodating competing heliconical and synclinic/anticlinic tendencies and produces a characteristic splitting of the resonant x-ray diffraction peaks into four signals symmetrically located around a signal of four-layer periodicity. These results reveal how bent dimers resolve local-packing-mode frustration through complex spontaneous hierarchical structural organization.
